subcategory: Header > Organisational header > White header with blue navigation
title: Header: White header with blue navigation
statement: You must have a Frutiger font licence to use an NHS organisational logo. Find out about using the Frutiger font , including registering for a free licence.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Header".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Header > Organisational header > Organisational logos
title: Header: Organisational logos
statement: Read more about creating NHS organisational logos in the NHS England identity guidelines . The organisational logo is an SVG (scalable vector graphic) and you can change the organisation name and descriptor in the code. Longer organisation names should be split onto 2 lines. You can also use a static asset, such as a PNG file.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Header".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Header > Progressive enhancement
title: Header: Progressive enhancement
statement: The header component uses progressive enhancement and requires JavaScript for enhanced functionality. When JavaScript is not available, users will not see the drop-down "More" button. Navigation links will be wrapped onto multiple lines.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Header".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Hint text > How to use hint text
title: Hint text: How to use hint text
statement: Use hint text to show information that helps the majority of users answer the question. Use it to give users help in context . Keep each hint to a single short phrase or sentence, without full stops. If you need to give a long, detailed explanation, do not use hint text. Screen readers will read out the entire text when users interact with the form element. This could frustrate users if the text is long. Do not use links in hint text. While screen readers will read out the link text, they usually do not tell users the text is a link. Do not use other interactive elements such as the details component in hint text. When screen reader users are in "form mode", they are unable to interact with the link in the component.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Hint text".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Hint text > How to use hint text > Radio items with hints
title: Hint text: Radio items with hints
statement: You can add hints to radios to give more information about the options.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Hint text".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Hint text > How to use hint text > Checkboxes with hint text
title: Hint text: Checkboxes with hint text
statement: Unlike with radios , users can select more than 1 option from a list of checkboxes . Do not assume that users will know how many options they can select.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Hint text".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Images > When to use images
title: Images: When to use images
statement: Informative images that meet real user needs can be very important on health services, especially where they help users identify specific health problems and get the treatment they need. We've also found users with some access needs (such as dyslexia) navigate health information through images. Images help them orient themselves and they separate out the content. But having unnecessary or decorative images can frustrate users, especially on information pages or transactional journeys.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Images".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Images > How to use images
title: Images: How to use images
statement: Images should flow with the text content, not appear too prominent or isolated. We recommend stacking images. We've found that gallery views (images side by side) confuse users.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Images".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Images > How to use images > Captions
title: Images: Captions
statement: The image component is made up of 2 elements: the image a caption underneath it in a white box Not all images need captions. If you use them: write a full sentence ending with a full stop keep captions short – ideally 1 sentence but no more than 2 start the caption with a number if the images show a sequence do not duplicate alt-text ( alternative text ) The caption assumes that the user can either see the image or read the alt-text. Use it to explain what you want users to conclude from it, for example, how serious their symptom is or what stage their condition has reached. In the above example, the alt-text is "Close-up of a person's tummy showing a number of creases in the skin under their belly button. Shown on light brown skin." The caption explains that stretch marks can be different colours and fade over time.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Images".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Images > How to use images > Accessibility
title: Images: Accessibility
statement: Do not use images that have words in them, because screen readers will not be able to read the words. Images must have text alternatives that describe the information or function they represent. This makes sure that people with disabilities can understand them. When using an image (or the img element), specify a text alternative with the alt attribute. Alt-text is not usually visible but is read out by screen readers or displayed if an image does not load or if images have been switched off. Read more about alt-text in the guidance on using alt-text for images in content . With complex images, like images of skin symptoms, long descriptions help people who face barriers due to sight loss. Find out how to provide a long description in our skin symptoms guidance .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Images".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Images > Research
title: Images: Research
statement: In testing we found gallery views (images side by side) confused users. Users either missed the images in the right hand column or they didn't know how to interpret the sequence. To get around this we recommend stacking images. We also found that users clicked images in gallery views, expecting them to appear larger in a pop-up modal. When we increased the size of the images and stacked them in 1 column (not 2), we didn't see anyone clicking on them to expand them.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Images".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Inset text > When to use inset text
title: Inset text: When to use inset text
statement: Use inset text for content that needs to stand out from the rest of the page.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Inset text".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Inset text > When not to use inset text
title: Inset text: When not to use inset text
statement: Do not use inset text in transactional pages. We haven't tested it there yet. Do not use inset text if you need to tell a user to contact their GP or get medical help. Use the pattern to help users decide when and where to get care (care cards) instead. Some users don't notice inset text on complex pages or near to other prominent elements, so we avoid using it for very important information that users need to see. Use a warning callout instead if the information: is time critical could have a significant effect on someone's health addresses a common or significant misconception or mistake
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Inset text".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Inset text > How to use inset text
title: Inset text: How to use inset text
statement: Don't overdo inset text. Think about whether you need it and the best place to put it.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Inset text".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Inset text > How to use inset text > Accessibility
title: Inset text: Accessibility
statement: People with visual disabilities may not be able to see the colour that marks out inset text. Instead they may rely on hidden labels to recognise it. We use Information: to let users with screen readers know that this is different to the body text.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Inset text".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Inset text > Research
title: Inset text: Research
statement: We've tested inset text in content pages and users understood its purpose. We haven't tested inset text in transactional pages. Get in touch to share your research findings if you've used this pattern.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Inset text".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Notification banners > When to use this component
title: Notification banners: When to use this component
statement: A notification banner lets you tell the user about something that's not directly relevant to the thing they're trying to do on that page of the service. There are 2 versions of the notification banner: the information banner (blue) the success banner (green) Use the information banner to tell the user about: something that affects the service as a whole (such as delays in processing applications or planned downtime) something that affects them in particular (for example, an approaching deadline they need to meet) Use the success banner to tell the user that something they've just done on a previous page was successful (for example, confirming that an email has been sent).
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Notification banners".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Notification banners > When not to use this component
title: Notification banners: When not to use this component
statement: Use notification banners sparingly. There's evidence that people often miss banners. Using them too often is likely to make this problem worse. See Banner blindness revisited by Nielsen Norman Group . Avoid showing more than 1 notification banner on the same page. Instead, combine the messages in a single notification banner. If the messages are too different to combine, decide which is your highest priority message and show that one. If the information is directly relevant to the thing the user is doing on that page, put the information in the main page content instead. If it needs to stand out, use: inset text component warning callout Do not use a notification banner to tell the user about validation errors. Use an error message component and error summary component instead. Do not show a notification banner and an error summary component on the same page. Just show the error summary.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Notification banners".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Notification banners > How it works
title: Notification banners: How it works
statement: Put the notification banner at top of the main container. If your page includes breadcrumbs or a back link, place it below these but before the h1 . The notification banner should be the same width as the page's other content, such as components, headings and body text. For example, if the other content takes up two-thirds of the screen on desktop devices, then the notification banner should also take up two-thirds. Read about page layout . Use role="region" and aria-labelledby="nhsuk-notification-banners-title" (with id="nhsuk-notification-banners-title" on <nhsuk-notification-banners__title> ) so that screen reader users can navigate to the notification banner.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Notification banners".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Notification banners > How it works > Notification banner headings
title: Notification banners: Notification banner headings
statement: The notification banner starts with a heading like "Important" or "Success". This is usually an <h2> . If you need a heading in the banner content, place it in <div class="nhsuk-notification-banner__content"> . It will normally be an <h3> . Do not use a heading for single line notifications. You can apply the nhsuk-notification-banners__heading class to a paragraph to make it stand out.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Notification banners".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Notification banners > Using the information banner
title: Notification banners: Using the information banner
statement: Use an information banner to tell users about something that affects the service as a whole. For example: in a service that lets the user apply for something, they might need to know that it's taking longer than usual to process applications in an account-type service, the user might need to know that the service will be down for scheduled maintenance If your service is getting more demand than usual, check that you've set up "There is a problem with the service" pages and "Service unavailable" pages, and the wording is up to date. Use the patterns in the GOV.UK design system . You can also use the information banner to tell users information about something that's happening elsewhere in the service. For example: in a case working system, the user might need to know that there are new cases waiting for their attention in an account-type service, you might need to tell the user that there's a deadline approaching or that a payment is overdue
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Notification banners".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Notification banners > Using the success banner
title: Notification banners: Using the success banner
statement: Use a success banner to confirm an action on a previous page was successful. For example, for steps in a long journey or small repeated tasks. Remove the success banner when the user moves to a new page. When the user finishes an entire journey, for example, a service that lets the user register for a thing, use a confirmation page , instead of a success banner. For long, complex services, use the task list component . You are unlikely to need a success banner on a page with a task list.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Notification banners".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Notification banners > Accessibility
title: Notification banners: Accessibility
statement: To make notification banners accessible: use a heading like "Success" so that you're not relying on colour alone to convey meaning (to meet WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.1 Use of colour ) use the same heading for banners across a service so that you're identifying components that work in the same way consistently (to meet WCAG 2.2 success criterion 3.2.4 Consistent identification ) the success banner includes role="alert" so the focus state shifts to the notification banner on page load.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Notification banners".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Pagination > When to use pagination
title: Pagination: When to use pagination
statement: Use pagination at the bottom of the page to help users navigate forwards and backwards through a series of related pages. For example, pages of search results or information about a health condition that's divided into multiple web pages. Consider using pagination when: showing all the content on a single page makes the page take too long to load or read most users only need the content on the 1st page or 1st few pages Use pagination rather than the "infinite scroll" technique which automatically loads content when the user approaches the bottom of the page. This causes problems for keyboard users.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Pagination".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Pagination > When not to use pagination
title: Pagination: When not to use pagination
statement: Only break up content onto separate pages if it improves the performance or usability of your service. Do not use pagination on pages which are not grouped together or "related" as this is likely to confuse users. Do not use pagination to navigate through a multi-page form. We use other components instead, including: buttons (usually a "Continue" button) to move forward back link to navigate back
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Pagination".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Pagination > How to use pagination
title: Pagination: How to use pagination
statement: Add the pagination component after the content on each page that you're paginating. Do not show pagination if there's only 1 page of content. Redirect users to the 1st page if they enter a URL of a page that no longer exists.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Pagination".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Pagination > How to use pagination > For navigating between content pages
title: Pagination: For navigating between content pages
statement: Use pagination at the bottom of pages of content to allow users to navigate around a topic that's divided into multiple pages (up to 8 pages). If you're using pagination at the bottom of content pages, you should also use a contents list at the top of the page. The 2 components make up the mini-hub pattern . Use the word "Previous" with an arrow left and a link to the previous page and the word "Next" with an arrow right and a link to the next page. Use the same page titles as in the contents list.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Pagination".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Pagination > How to use pagination > For navigating between pages of items
title: Pagination: For navigating between pages of items
statement: Use numbered pagination if users need to navigate through pages of similar items. For example, a list of search results or a list of cases in a case working system. Decide the maximum number of items to show on each page based on the context of your service and the amount of content for each item. Show the page number in the page <title> so that screen reader users know they've navigated to a different page. For example, "Search results (page 1 of 4)". The pagination should always show the page numbers for: the current page the page before the current page the page after the current page 1st and last pages For larger screens, you can show the page numbers for 2 or more pages before and after the current page. Use ellipses (…) to show gaps in the page numbering. For example: [1] 2 … 100 1 [2] 3 … 100 1 2 [3] 4 … 100 1 2 3 [4] 5 … 100 1 … 4 [5] 6 … 100 1 … 97 [98] 99 100 1 … 98 [99] 100 1 … 99 [100] Do not show the previous page link on the 1st page and do not show the next page link on the last page.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Pagination".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Pagination > How to use pagination > Accessibility
title: Pagination: Accessibility
statement: The pagination components are surrounded by a <nav> element to show that they are navigation links. This element has an aria-label attribute with the value Pagination . Screen readers that support this attribute will read this. There is also a visually hidden heading title pagination which will be read by screen readers as a heading to the links. If the link describes the current page that you are on, then it has the aria-current="page" value to indicate to screen readers that this is the case.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Pagination".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Pagination > Research > Content page navigation
title: Pagination: Content page navigation
statement: We tested content page pagination in grouped information pages in 3 labs in 2018. We have not tested it in forms. 4 out of 5 users, including a user with a very low level of digital skill, used pagination to navigate through the pages. They understood that it was associated with the navigation at the top of the page. Users found that the pagination reflected the way they read content and their mental model of the structure of the content.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Pagination".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Pagination > Research > Numbered page navigation
title: Pagination: Numbered page navigation
statement: GOV.UK based their component for navigating between pages of items on similar ones developed and used successfully by the Government Digital Service, Ministry of Justice and the Home Office.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Pagination".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Panel > When to use a panel
title: Panel: When to use a panel
statement: Use the panel component to display important information. There are 2 versions of this component: the green panel , used on confirmation pages to tell the user they have successfully completed the transaction the blue interruption panel , used on interruption pages to pause a user's journey with important information
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Panel".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Panel > When not to use a panel
title: Panel: When not to use a panel
statement: Never use the panel component to highlight important information in body content. Instead consider using: inset text a warning callout the pattern to help users decide when and where to get care (care cards)
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Panel".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Panel > Blue interruption panel
title: Panel: Blue interruption panel
statement: If you need to pause a user's journey with important information, use an interruption panel. Read how to use it in the interruption page pattern .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Panel".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Password input > When to use password input
title: Password input: When to use password input
statement: Use this component whenever you need users to create or enter a password. Before using this component, read: the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) guidance on password administration for system owners (including their password policy ) and NHS England's multi-factor authentication (MFA) policy about using NHS login and Care Identity Service (NHS England) for authentication
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Password input".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Password input > When not to use password input
title: Password input: When not to use password input
statement: Do not use this component to ask for any information other than a password. Use a text input component to ask for other security information, such as: multi-factor authentication codes answers to security questions other personally identifiable information Also see GOV.UK's Confirm a phone number pattern .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Password input".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Password input > How to use password input
title: Password input: How to use password input
statement: This component lets users enter a password, with an option to show what they've entered as plain text. This allows users to visually check their password before they submit it, which helps them reduce errors and choose passwords that are more unique and secure. Use this guidance with GOV.UK's Ask users for passwords pattern , which explains how to help users create and enter secure and memorable passwords.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Password input".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Password input > How to use password input > Error messages
title: Password input: Error messages
statement: If the user enters their account details incorrectly, do not reveal whether they got the username or password wrong. Clear any information entered into the password input. Revealing the source of the error can help fraudsters break into people's accounts. See how to handle incorrect login attempts and help users who forget their password in GOV.UK's Ask users for passwords pattern .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Password input".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Password input > How to use password input > Showing and hiding passwords
title: Password input: Showing and hiding passwords
statement: Hide the password by default until the user chooses to show it using the "Show" button. Users might not be in a private space when entering or creating a password, so hide passwords by default. If you do choose to include 2 or more password inputs on a page, the "Show" and "Hide" toggles and labels for each password input must be different. For example, you can label: the 1st input as "Password" with a toggle of "Show password" the 2nd input as "Re-enter password" with a toggle of "Show re-entered password"
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Password input".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Password input > How to use password input > Avoid adding a "confirm password" field
title: Password input: Avoid adding a "confirm password" field
statement: It's not necessary to add a 2nd password field, also known as a "confirm password" field, particularly as this component allows users to show and hide passwords.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Password input".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Password input > How to use password input > Define the input's type as "password"
title: Password input: Define the input's type as "password"
statement: If the form is submitted when the input's text is visible, JavaScript will change the input type back to password . You must check this happens automatically. This is to prevent browsers from remembering it as a value the user has entered before and potentially displaying it as an autofill option on non-password inputs.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Password input".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Password input > How to use password input > Use the autocomplete attribute
title: Password input: Use the autocomplete attribute
statement: Use the autocomplete attribute on password inputs to help users complete forms faster. Autocomplete indicates to browsers and password managers what kind of password is needed so it can be entered for the user. Set the autocomplete attribute to new-password if the user is creating a password. Otherwise, use current-password . Many browsers will autofill password inputs, even when the autocomplete attribute is missing or set to off .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Password input".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Password input > How to use password input > Allow copy and paste
title: Password input: Allow copy and paste
statement: The NCSC recommends that online services let people: use password managers copy and paste passwords Users can copy any text from a password field when it's set on "Show". This is a feature of browser behaviour and cannot be overridden. This can be useful for users, for example to save a password that the browser has suggested into a separate password manager.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Password input".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Password input > How to use password input > Avoid restricting the user's input
title: Password input: Avoid restricting the user's input
statement: Support all the characters users may need to enter a password, including numbers and symbols. Set a minimum length of at least 12 characters. If you need to set a maximum password length on the server to prevent buffer overflow attacks without discouraging strong passwords, allow at least 64 characters. The NCSC password policy includes advice on technical solutions and reducing the burden on users. Any restrictions must be identical wherever the user creates or enters a password. If you change the restrictions over time, you must continue to support existing user passwords or ask them to set a new one. Users will not get any feedback when they've reached the maxlength and their text input has been truncated. This happens when a user has pasted text from elsewhere or it's been autofilled by a password manager. If a user exceeds the maximum length, show an error message instead. See GOV.UK's pattern for helping users to recover from validation errors .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Password input".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Password input > Progressive enhancement
title: Password input: Progressive enhancement
statement: The password input component uses progressive enhancement and requires JavaScript for enhanced functionality. When JavaScript is not available, users will see their browser's native password input without the "Show" button.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Password input".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Radios > When not to use radios
title: Radios: When not to use radios
statement: Do not use radios if users might need to select more than 1 option. Use checkboxes instead.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Radios".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Radios > How to use radios
title: Radios: How to use radios
statement: Position radios to the left of their labels. This makes them easier to find, especially for users of screen magnifiers. Unlike with checkboxes, users can only select 1 option from a list of radios. Do not assume that users will know how many options they can select based on the visual difference between radios and checkboxes alone. If needed, add a hint explaining this, for example, "Select 1 option". Do not pre-select radio options as this makes it more likely that users will: not realise they've missed a question submit the wrong answer Users cannot go back to having no option selected once they have selected an option, without refreshing their browser window. So you should include "None of these" or "I do not know" if they are valid options. In any case, it's best to beware binary choices . Order radio options alphabetically by default. In some cases, it's helpful to order them from most-to-least common options, for example, by population size. But be careful, as this can reinforce bias. If in doubt, order alphabetically. Group radios together in a <fieldset> with a <legend> that describes them. You can see an example at the top of this page. This is usually a question, like "Are you 18 or over?". Read more about using fieldset .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Radios".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Radios > How to use radios > Inline radios
title: Radios: Inline radios
statement: In some cases, you can choose to display radios "inline" beside one another (horizontally). Only use inline radios when: the question only has 2 options both options are short On small screens such as mobile devices, the radios will still be "stacked" on top of one another (vertically).
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Radios".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Radios > How to use radios > Radios with hints
title: Radios: Radios with hints
statement: Use hint text to give users help in context . Read more about hint text . Do not assume that users will know that they can only select 1 option based on the visual difference between radios and checkboxes. If needed, add a hint explaining this, for example, "Select 1 option".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Radios".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Radios > How to use radios > Radio items with hints
title: Radios: Radio items with hints
statement: You can add hints to radios to give more information about the options.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Radios".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Radios > How to use radios > Radio items with a text divider
title: Radios: Radio items with a text divider
statement: If 1 or more of your radio options is different from the others, it can help users if you separate them using a text divider. The text is usually the word "or".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Radios".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Radios > How to use radios > Smaller radios
title: Radios: Smaller radios
statement: Use standard-sized radios in most cases. You can use small radios where you need something less visually prominent. For example, on: a page of search results where users need to see and change search filters without distracting them from the results on information-dense screens in services designed for repeat use, like staff-facing systems
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Radios".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Radios > How to use radios > Error messages
title: Radios: Error messages
statement: Display an error message if the user has not: selected any radios answered a conditionally revealed question Style error messages like this. Follow: our guidance on error messages GOV.UK design system guidance on error messages for radios
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Radios".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Radios > Progressive enhancement
title: Radios: Progressive enhancement
statement: The radios component uses progressive enhancement and requires JavaScript for enhanced functionality. When JavaScript is not available, conditionally revealed content will be revealed by default.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Radios".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Radios > Research
title: Radios: Research
statement: Our radios are based on the GOV.UK design system. Read a GOV.UK blog post about their updates to radios and checkboxes .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Radios".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Review date
title: Review date
statement: Go to the pattern to reassure users that a page is up to date .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Review date".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Search input > When to use search input
title: Search input: When to use search input
statement: Use the search input component to help users find a topic, person, task, place or other type of record when navigation alone is not practical. You can enable search in the header component . Use this to provide a global search.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Search input".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Search input > When not to use search input
title: Search input: When not to use search input
statement: Do not rely on search in place of a well-structured information architecture and navigation. Consider using sorting or filtering alongside or instead of search.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Search input".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Search input > How to use search input
title: Search input: How to use search input
statement: Use hint text to give users help in context . Read more about hint text .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Search input".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Search input > How to use search input > Cross icon
title: Search input: Cross icon
statement: When a user types into the input, a cross icon button appears which allows users to clear the input. This is an enhancement for browsers that support it. Some browsers such as Firefox do not show it.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Search input".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Search input > How to use search input > Text label
title: Search input: Text label
statement: The search button can include a text label. For example, you can use "Find" to: differentiate it from other searches in the same service communicate that this will match only 1 result and take you directly to it
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Search input".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Search input > How to use search input > Secondary button
title: Search input: Secondary button
statement: Depending on the hierarchy of the page, the search input can use a secondary button.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Search input".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Search input > How to use search input > Large search input
title: Search input: Large search input
statement: The search input can be large, depending on the context of the page. For example, you can use a large input on a dedicated search page.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Search input".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Select > When to use select
title: Select: When to use select
statement: The select component should only be used as a last resort in public-facing services because research shows that some users find selects very difficult to use.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Select".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Select > When not to use select
title: Select: When not to use select
statement: The select component allows users to choose an option from a long list. Before using the select component, try asking users other questions which will allow you to present them with fewer options. Consider using a different solution, such as radios .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Select".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Select > How to use select
title: Select: How to use select
statement: If you use the component for settings, you can make an option pre-selected by default when users first see it. If you use the component for questions, do not pre-select any of the options in case it influences users' answers.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Select".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Select > How to use select > Select with hint
title: Select: Select with hint
statement: You can add hint text to help the user understand the options and choose 1 of them.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Select".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Select > How to use select > Error messages
title: Select: Error messages
statement: Display an error message if the user has not selected an option. Style error messages as shown in the example:
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Select".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Select > Research
title: Select: Research
statement: User research shows that some users struggle with the select component, especially people who use a keyboard to navigate and people with motor difficulties. The dropdown feature makes users work hard to see and understand their options and click the option they want.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Select".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Skip link > When to use a skip link
title: Skip link: When to use a skip link
statement: All nhs.uk pages must include a skip link in the header following guidance in the GOV.UK Design System .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Skip link".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Skip link > How skip links work
title: Skip link: How skip links work
statement: Some people use the tab key on their keyboard to navigate through the links and form elements on a web page. Including a skip link gives users the option to bypass the top-level navigation links and jump to the main content on the page. The skip link component is visually hidden until a keyboard press activates it.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Skip link".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Skip link > Research
title: Skip link: Research
statement: If you've used skip links, please share your user research findings.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Skip link".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Summary list > When to use summary lists
title: Summary list: When to use summary lists
statement: Use the summary list component to present pairs of related information, known as key-value pairs, in a list, where: the key is a label, like "Name" the value is the piece of information itself, like "John Smith" Think about how you can use the summary list along with other components or patterns to give users a sense of control. You can use it to summarise a user's responses at the end of a form, for example as part of the check answers pattern .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Summary list".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Summary list > When not to use summary lists
title: Summary list: When not to use summary lists
statement: The summary list uses the description list <dl> HTML element, so only use it to present information that has a key and at least 1 value. Do not use it for tabular data or a simple list of information or tasks, like a task list page. (See the complete multiple tasks pattern .) For those, use a <table> , <ul> or <ol> .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Summary list".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Summary list > How to use summary lists > Summary list with actions
title: Summary list: Summary list with actions
statement: You can add actions to a summary list, like a "Change" link to let users go back and edit their answer. If you do this, make sure information they have already entered is pre-populated. People who use assistive technology, like a screen reader, may hear the links out of context and not know what they do. To give more context, add visually hidden text to the links. This means a screen reader user will hear a meaningful action, like "Change name" or "Change date of birth".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Summary list".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Summary list > How to use summary lists > Summary list without actions or borders
title: Summary list: Summary list without actions or borders
statement: If you do not include actions in your summary list and it would be better for your design to remove the separating borders, use the nhsuk-summary-list--no-border class. To remove borders on a single row, use the nhsuk-summary-list__row--no-border class.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Summary list".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Summary list > Summary cards
title: Summary list: Summary cards
statement: If you're showing multiple summary lists on a page, you can show each list within a summary card. This lets you visually separate each summary list and give each a title and some actions. Use summary cards when you need to show: multiple summary lists that all describe the same type of thing, such as people actions that will apply to all the items in a list Summary cards are often used in case working systems to help users quickly view a set of information and related actions. Do not use summary cards if you only need to show a small amount of related information. Use summary lists instead, and structure them with headings if needed. If you're showing summary cards at the end of a longer journey, you might want to familiarise the user with them earlier on, such as when the user reviews individual sections.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Summary list".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Summary list > Summary cards > Card titles
title: Summary list: Card titles
statement: Use the summary card's header area to give each summary list a title. Each title must be unique and help identify what the summary list describes. For example, this could be the name of a specific person, organisation or professional qualification. Try to keep titles short and relevant. You can use 1 or 2 important values in the summary list, such as the first and last name of a person. The example uses the nhsuk-summary-list__row--no-border class to remove the bottom border of the last row.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Summary list".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Summary list > Summary cards > Card actions
title: Summary list: Card actions
statement: You can add card actions in the header, which will be shown after the summary card's title. For example, if you have multiple rows with "change" actions that all take the user to the same place, you can show a single "change" card action instead. This helps avoid repeating the same row action on every row. Card actions are shown in bold text to make them visually distinct from row actions. They help alert the user that the card action will affect the entire summary card. Write link text for card actions to tell the user what the card action will do and that it will apply to the entire summary card. It should also be as short as possible, usually 2 words. Example card actions include: remove appointment edit appointment update issue approve application cancel order Keep it short and do not add more than 2 to 3 actions in a header. If a card action cannot easily be undone or might have serious consequences, consider adding a warning or asking the user for confirmation.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Summary list".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table
title: Table
statement: We have 6 kinds of table: basic compact striped responsive scrolling sortable The page also explains how to: use word breaks in a table display missing data display tables on dark backgrounds
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table > When to use a table
title: Table: When to use a table
statement: Use a table to: present data or information that can be organised in a structured way make it easy for users to scan and compare information and understand relationships between data Aim to present a minimum of data. If you have a lot of data, try to organise it into multiple tables or multiple pages.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table > When not to use a table
title: Table: When not to use a table
statement: Use tables with caution. They may not be the best way to present information, especially for the public and on mobile screens. In staff services, complex data tables can lead to cognitive overload, a poor user experience and performance issues. There may be better ways to meet users' needs, for example: a plain English summary with headings and lists an expander tabs Check this in your user research. Do not use a table to lay out content on a page. Use the grid system instead.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table > Basic table > or more column table
title: Table: or more column table
statement: If you have numeric data, right align the column header and cells to make it easier to compare numbers: in Nunjucks, add the format: "numeric" option to the column header for HTML, add the nhsuk-table__header--numeric class to the column header and nhsuk-table__cell--numeric class to the cells If you have non-numeric data that you want to right align: in Nunjucks, add the align: "right" option to the column header for HTML, add the nhsuk-u-text-align-right override class to both the column header and cells
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table > Basic table > When not to use a basic table
title: Table: When not to use a basic table
statement: Do not use a basic table if your table content becomes squashed and hard to read on small screens. Use a responsive table instead.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table > Compact table
title: Table: Compact table
statement: Use a compact table when you have a lot of data to display. It reduces the vertical padding between rows, making it easier to scan the data. If you're using Nunjucks, add the compact: true option. For HTML add the nhsuk-table--compact class to the table. Try first to reduce the amount of data you display, for example by splitting it into multiple tables or combining columns. For example, showing a name and NHS number together in 1 column.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table > Striped table
title: Table: Striped table
statement: Add striping (sometimes called zebra stripes) to tables with many rows and columns of data to help users distinguish between rows. If you're using Nunjucks, add the striped: true option. For HTML add the nhsuk-table--striped class to the table.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table > Responsive table
title: Table: Responsive table
statement: This table has a responsive layout. On large screens it displays horizontally but on small screens it stacks vertically. Use a responsive table when your table becomes squashed and hard to read on small screens, 768px and smaller. If you're using Nunjucks, add the responsive: true option. For HTML add the nhsuk-table--responsive class to the table and set the correct role attribute for each element of the table.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table > Responsive table > When not to use a responsive table
title: Table: When not to use a responsive table
statement: Do not use a responsive table if your content is easier to read and understand on a small screen in a non-stacked layout. Use a basic table instead. If you have too many columns to fit, use a scrolling table.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table > Scrolling table
title: Table: Scrolling table
statement: Add the scrolling container when your table has many columns and you cannot split it up or use a responsive table. If you're using Nunjucks, add the scroll: true option. For HTML add the scrolling container from the example below. The example uses an nhsuk-scroll container to automatically toggle left or right shadows when scrolling.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table > Sortable table
title: Table: Sortable table
statement: A sortable table lets users sort columns in ascending or descending order, alphabetically or numerically. Ascending order (up arrow) arranges: numerical data from the lowest to the highest value text in alphabetical order A to Z Descending order (down arrow) reverses this. This table only sorts by 1 column at a time. Sortable columns show a double arrow until they're sorted. When users click in the column header of an unsorted column, it sorts and shows a single arrow. Clicking again toggles between ascending and descending.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table > Sortable table > When to use a sortable table
title: Table: When to use a sortable table
statement: Use this table when users need to analyse and prioritise data.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table > Sortable table > How to use a sortable table
title: Table: How to use a sortable table
statement: Carry out user research to understand what your users need to do with the data and if a sortable table is the best way to meet their needs. There are 2 ways to sort a table. You can: sort data that fits on 1 page sort more than 1 page of data The sortable table component uses JavaScript to sort the data in the user's browser. Use it where you have only 1 page of data. Make sure your data has a suitable sort order if JavaScript does not run. By default when you click on the column header for an unsorted column, it will sort that column in ascending order. To apply descending order when clicked: in Nunjucks, add the sortNext: "descending" option to the column header for HTML, add the data-sort-next="descending" attribute to the column header Typically users expect text to sort A to Z by default. With numbers, they often expect them to sort with the biggest number first. Do not allow sorting on columns that cannot be meaningfully ordered, for example comments from users. Do not add code to automatically save the sort order. Users may not expect this and it could add clinical risk. A page refresh or navigation must return the page to its default sort order, unless you add functionality to allow users to save their sort order explicitly. By default, columns will be sorted as text. To correctly order columns containing numbers: in Nunjucks, add the format: "numeric" option to the column header for HTML, add the nhsuk-table__header--numeric class to the column header and nhsuk-table__cell--numeric class to the cells Columns set to numeric will work correctly with most number symbols, including commas, decimals, percentages and currencies. Use numeric for dates. You can override the default sort value to make the presented data easier for users to understand. For example: dates: 30 November 2026 sorted as 2026-11-30 months: January sorted as 01 January prefixes: The Whittington Hospital sorted as Whittington Hospital To override the default sort value: in Nunjucks, add the sortValue option to the table cell for HTML, add the data-sort-value attribute to the table cell Make sure to override the sort value for missing data . For example, setting sortValue: "£0" will sort the text "No data" consistently with other cells. In this example the default sort order is by amount spent (descending). If your table is paginated, sorting should be applied server-side across all pages. Do not sort the current page only. Use server-side sorting by adding a link to the column head
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table > Using word-breaks in a table
title: Table: Using word-breaks in a table
statement: To avoid very long words, such as email addresses, breaking the layout of a table, you can use word-breaks. To do this: in Nunjucks, add the class: "nhsuk-u-text-break-word" option to the table cell for HTML, add the nhsuk-u-text-break-word override class to the table cell Find out more about word-breaks, with or without a hyphen, in breaking up long words in the typography section .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table > Displaying missing data
title: Table: Displaying missing data
statement: Do not leave empty cells in your table. The only exception can be the top left cell. If you have missing data, include some short text to explain why it's missing, such as: "No data" "Not applicable" "Not known" To distinguish missing data from other table content, make the text dark grey by adding the class: "nhsuk-u-secondary-text-colour" Nunjucks option to the table cell. For HTML set it via the class attribute.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table > Tables on dark backgrounds
title: Table: Tables on dark backgrounds
statement: To show tables with white text on dark backgrounds, add the variant: "reverse" option using Nunjucks. For HTML add the nhsuk-table--reverse class to the table. Make sure all users can see the table content. The background colour must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 with white to meet WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (minimum), level AA (W3C) .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table > Accessibility
title: Table: Accessibility
statement: Follow WebAIM's guidance for tables and: give tables captions use the scope attribute to associate the data cells with the appropriate headers let the browser window determine the width of the table whenever possible, to reduce horizontal scrolling
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table > Accessibility > Table captions
title: Table: Table captions
statement: Use the <caption> element to describe a table in the same way you would use a heading. A caption helps users find, navigate and understand tables. Style table captions to match the visual hierarchy of your page's content. If you're using Nunjucks, add the size: "l" option to the caption. For HTML add the nhsuk-table__caption--l class to the caption. You can use sizes s , m , l , xl .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table > Accessibility > Table headers
title: Table: Table headers
statement: Use table headers to tell users what the rows and columns represent.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table > Accessibility > Sortable tables
title: Table: Sortable tables
statement: The sortable table tells screen reader users that it can be sorted. When the user sorts the table, it announces what the new sort order is.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table > Research > Basic table
title: Table: Basic table
statement: This table tested well with users of health information on the NHS website.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table > Research > Sortable table
title: Table: Sortable table
statement: This table was developed by NHS England and tested in the Run breast screening in England and Manage vaccinations in schools services. There is an overlap between sortable tables and: search filter pagination We want to understand better how they can work together. We have not yet developed a responsive or scrolling sortable table. If you need a responsive sorting table, you could try adding a select component . Please feed back if you develop any of these or implement server-side sorting.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Table > Research > Table in a card
title: Table: Table in a card
statement: We have also included an example of a table in a card in the NHS.UK frontend (in GitHub) . We have not published it in this list of components yet because it needs more testing.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Table".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Tabs > When to use tabs
title: Tabs: When to use tabs
statement: Tabs can be a helpful way of letting users quickly switch between related information if: your content can be usefully separated into clearly labelled sections the 1st section is more relevant than the others for most users users will not need to view all the sections at once Tabs can work well for people who use a service regularly, for example, staff using a patient record system. Their need to perform tasks quickly may be greater than their need for simplicity of first-time use. Test your content without tabs first. Consider if it's better to: simplify and reduce the amount of content split the content across multiple pages keep the content on a single page, separated by headings use a table of contents to let users navigate quickly to specific sections of content
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Tabs".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Tabs > When not to use tabs
title: Tabs: When not to use tabs
statement: Do not use the tabs component if the total amount of content the tabs contain will make the page slow to load. For this reason, do not use the tabs component as a form of page navigation. Tabs hide content from users and not everyone will notice them or understand how they work. Do not use tabs if your users might need to: read through all of the content in order, for example, to understand a step-by-step process compare information in different tabs, because having to memorise information and switch backwards and forwards can be difficult
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Tabs".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Tabs > Decide between using tabs, expanders and the details component
title: Tabs: Decide between using tabs, expanders and the details component
statement: Tabs, expanders , and details all hide sections of content which a user can choose to reveal. If you decide to use 1 of these components, consider if: the user needs to view more than 1 section at a time – if not, use tabs the user needs to switch quickly between sections – tabs can show content without pushing other sections down the page, unlike expanders you have 7 or more sections of content – tabs are arranged horizontally, so may not work well, while expanders are arranged vertically there are only 1 or 2 sections of short, less important content – the details component is more suitable as it's visually smaller and less prominent than an expander or tabs
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Tabs".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Tabs > How to use tabs
title: Tabs: How to use tabs
statement: There are 2 ways to use the tabs component. You can use HTML or, if you're using Nunjucks or the NHS.UK Prototype Kit , you can use the Nunjucks macro.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Tabs".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Tabs > How to use tabs > Use clear labels
title: Tabs: Use clear labels
statement: Tabs hide content, so the tab labels need to make it very clear what they link to. Otherwise users will not know if they need to click on them. If you struggle to come up with clear labels, it might be because the way you've separated the content is not clear.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Tabs".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Tabs > How to use tabs > Order the tabs according to user needs
title: Tabs: Order the tabs according to user needs
statement: The 1st tab should be the most commonly needed section. Arrange the other tabs in the order that makes most sense for your users.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Tabs".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Tabs > How to use tabs > Do not disable tabs
title: Tabs: Do not disable tabs
statement: Disabling elements is normally confusing for users. If there is no content for a tab, either remove the tab or, if that would be confusing for your users, explain why there is no content when the tab is selected.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Tabs".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Tabs > How to use tabs > Avoid tabs that wrap over more than 1 line
title: Tabs: Avoid tabs that wrap over more than 1 line
statement: If you use too many tabs or they have long labels then they may wrap over more than 1 line. This makes it harder for users to see the connection between the selected tab and its content.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Tabs".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Tabs > Accessibility
title: Tabs: Accessibility
statement: Keyboard users should be able to move focus between tabs using arrow keys and select a tab by pressing enter. Screen reader users should hear which tab is currently focused, how many tabs there are and whether the current tab is open.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Tabs".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Tabs > Progressive enhancement
title: Tabs: Progressive enhancement
statement: The tabs component uses progressive enhancement and requires JavaScript for enhanced functionality. When JavaScript is not available, users will see the tabbed content on a single page, in order from 1st to last, with a table of contents that links to each of the sections. This is also how the component currently behaves on small screens, but more research is needed on this.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Tabs".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Tabs > Research and testing
title: Tabs: Research and testing
statement: The Government Digital Service (GDS) developed and tested the tabs component. Several NHS services are using tabs but we need to know more about how they test with users. For example, we need to know: which types of services tabs work best in that this approach to tabs is the best option for screen reader users and sighted keyboard users how this component should behave on small screen sizes
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Tabs".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Tag > When to use a tag
title: Tag: When to use a tag
statement: Use the tag component when it's possible for something to have more than 1 status and it's useful for the user to know about that status. For example, you can use a tag to show whether an item in a task list has been "completed".
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Tag".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Tag > How it works
title: Tag: How it works
statement: Tags are just used to indicate a status. Do not add links. Use adjectives rather than verbs for the names of your tags. Using a verb might make a user think that clicking on them will do something.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Tag".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Tag > How it works > Showing 1 or 2 statuses
title: Tag: Showing 1 or 2 statuses
statement: Sometimes a single status is enough. For example, if you need to tell users which parts of an application they've finished and which they have not, you may only need a "Completed" tag. Because the user understands that if something does not have a tag, that means it's incomplete. Or it can make sense to have 2 statuses. For example, you may find that you need 1 tag for "Active" users and 1 for "Inactive" users.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Tag".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Tag > How it works > Showing multiple statuses
title: Tag: Showing multiple statuses
statement: Tags should be helpful to users. The more you add, the harder it is for users to remember them. So start with the smallest number of statuses you think might work, then add more if your user research shows there's a need for them.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Tag".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Tag > How it works > Using colour with tags
title: Tag: Using colour with tags
statement: You can use colour to help distinguish between different tags – or to help draw the user's attention to a tag if it's especially important. For example, it makes sense to use nhsuk-tag--red for a tag that reads "Urgent". Do not rely on colour alone to convey information because it's not accessible. If you use the same tag in more than 1 place, make sure you keep the colour consistent. Because tags with solid colours tend to stand out more, it's usually best to avoid mixing solid colours and tints: use one or the other. This matters less if you're only using 2 colours. For example, it's okay to use the tint nhsuk-tag--grey and solid blue tags together if you only need 2 statuses. We use a border of the same colour as the tag text to stand out against the NHS page background colour.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Tag".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Tag > How it works > Additional colours
title: Tag: Additional colours
statement: If you need more tag colours, you can use the following tints.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Tag".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Tag > Accessibility
title: Tag: Accessibility
statement: All contrasts between text and background meet level AAA of WCAG 2.0. Read more about accessibility and colour .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Tag".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Tag > Research
title: Tag: Research
statement: We have tested tags in the NHS e-referral service, the "Submit your electronic declaration" service and the NHS App prescriptions service. We found that they helped users: make a decision about whether or not to proceed with their journey understand their progress or the status of an order save time as they could see the information they needed quickly We also found that it helped to use sentence case rather than block capitals for readability.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Tag".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Task list
title: Task list
statement: The task list component displays all the tasks a user needs to do, and allows users to easily identify which ones are done and which they still need to do.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Task list".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Task list > When to use the task list
title: Task list: When to use the task list
statement: If your users have to get through a long or complex service, use the task list to give them more control. For example, if some users cannot complete the tasks in one sitting. You can also use a task list to allow users to complete tasks in the order they choose. This will help them plan their time and complete sections as and when they can.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Task list".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Task list > When not to use the task list
title: Task list: When not to use the task list
statement: Try to simplify the service before you use a task list. If you're able to reduce the number of tasks or steps involved, you might not need one. Do not use the task list as a way of showing users their answers. For this, use a summary list instead.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Task list".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Task list > How the task list works
title: Task list: How the task list works
statement: Where possible, let users complete tasks in whatever order they like. The status alongside the task indicates whether they can start it. Users can select a task to start completing it. Once they have completed it and returned to the task list, the status for that task will have changed to "Completed". Users can only move on from the task list when all tasks are shown as "Completed". Find more information about how to use the task list in a service in the complete multiple tasks pattern guidance .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Task list".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Task list > How the task list works > Tasks
title: Task list: Tasks
statement: Tasks are usually actions that the user needs to take to complete a service. Each task in a task list includes a task name and a status. It can also include hint text if you decide this is needed. The whole row turns grey on hover to show that it is linked, allowing users to select anywhere in it to start the task. The task name gives users a reasonable expectation of what that task is about. For example, "Your contact details" or "Upload evidence". Use sentence case and keep it short. Users of screen readers might find it difficult to navigate the task list if the task names are too long. If you're finding it difficult to come up with a clear and concise task name, it might be because the task itself is too complex and may need to be separated into smaller tasks. Group questions and actions into tasks in a way that makes sense to users, based on their needs. Only use hint text if there is evidence that the user needs more information about what the task will include. Keep hint text to a single, short sentence. Screen readers read out the entire text when users interact with the task link. This could frustrate users if the text is long. Do not include links in the hint text. The whole task row links users to the task itself, so any links in the hint text will not work. If there are a lot of tasks to complete, you might find that grouping them makes it easier for users to understand and plan what they need to do. Tasks can be grouped into separate task lists on a page. Give each task list a short heading that clearly explains the grouping. Find more information on grouping tasks in the complete multiple tasks pattern guidance .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Task list".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Task list > How the task list works > Statuses
title: Task list: Statuses
statement: Statuses use colour and a short descriptor to give users a quick overview of how much of the task list they have completed, and how much is left to do. Find more information on how to show statuses in the complete multiple tasks pattern guidance .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Task list".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Task list > Research on the task list
title: Task list: Research on the task list
statement: The GOV.UK design system developed and tested this component. Find out more about their research on the GOV.UK task list page . If you are using this component in a service, we would like to hear about any user research so that we can identify any potential issues.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Task list".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Text input > When to use the text input component
title: Text input: When to use the text input component
statement: Use the text input component when you need users to enter text that's no longer than a single line, such as their name or phone number.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Text input".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Text input > When not to use the text input component
title: Text input: When not to use the text input component
statement: Do not use this component if you need users to enter longer answers that might span several lines. In this case, use the textarea component .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Text input".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Text input > Research
title: Text input: Research
statement: If you've used text input, please share your user research findings.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Text input".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Textarea > When to use textarea
title: Textarea: When to use textarea
statement: Use textarea when you want users to enter multiple lines of text. Use it when you are confident that users will: input the information you need not input information that could cause clinical or safeguarding concerns, for example, details of medical symptoms or harmful behaviour that your service is not designed to deal with If you are not sure about this, talk with your clinical team. Textarea can cause problems as users may: find open questions difficult to answer input information that's difficult to analyse disclose personal information, for example, about their symptoms or situation and expect you to reply quickly They may ignore messages in hint text such as "Do not include personal information like your name, date of birth or NHS number". Consider other ways to collect the information you need. Use structured, closed questions if possible. For example, let users select from options using radios or checkboxes .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Textarea".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Textarea > When not to use textarea
title: Textarea: When not to use textarea
statement: If you want users to enter a single line answer, such as a phone number or name, use text input . Only use textarea if your team has considered the alternatives and agreed that it's the best way to meet user and business needs.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Textarea".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Textarea > How to use textarea > Understand and manage the risks
title: Textarea: Understand and manage the risks
statement: Users sometimes use open text boxes to report health concerns or difficult circumstances that are not relevant to your service, even if you ask them not to. Your team must monitor and respond to any clinical safety or safeguarding concerns. If you cannot do this, it can leave: users in unsafe situations staff feeling stressed and uncertain what to do the organisation facing reputational harm or legal action for not acting on information Read our guidance on making sure you need each question . If you use textarea in a public service, make sure you: assess the risks talk with your clinical and legal teams if relevant, set expectations at the start that your service cannot respond to information about an individual's medical situation and signpost to GPs or 111 make your question as specific as possible and consider setting a character limit put in place a process for monitoring and dealing with safety issues, including over weekends and holidays set up technical safeguards, for example to detect inappropriate content Read more about managing clinical risk in NHS service standard 16: Make your service clinically safe .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Textarea".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Textarea > How to use textarea > Label textareas
title: Textarea: Label textareas
statement: You must label textareas. Do not use placeholder text for a label, as it disappears when users click inside the textarea. Align labels above the textarea they refer to. Labels should be short, direct and written in sentence case. Do not use colons at the end of labels.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Textarea".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Textarea > How to use textarea > Use the right size of textarea
title: Textarea: Use the right size of textarea
statement: Make the height of a textarea proportional to the amount of text you expect users to enter. You can set the height of a textarea by specifying the rows attribute. If you are using a large textarea in a public service, with or without character count , be aware that giving users more space may increase clinical risk.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Textarea".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Textarea > How to use textarea > Using hint text
title: Textarea: Using hint text
statement: Use hint text to give users help in context , for example, tell users what information to include or not to include. But bear in mind that users may ignore this, especially in public services. Read more about hint text .
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Textarea".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Textarea > How to use textarea > Do not disable copy and paste
title: Textarea: Do not disable copy and paste
statement: Users will often need to copy and paste information into a textarea, so do not stop them doing this.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Textarea".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Textarea > How to use textarea > Error messages
title: Textarea: Error messages
statement: Style error messages like this. Follow: our guidance on error messages GOV.UK design system guidance on textarea error messages
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Textarea".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Textarea > Research
title: Textarea: Research
statement: We tested the textarea component on a "Register with a GP" prototype at 2 labs in December 2018. Users understood the purpose of the textarea and were able to use it.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Textarea".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Warning callout > When to use a warning callout
title: Warning callout: When to use a warning callout
statement: Use this callout for information that: is time critical could have a significant effect on someone's health addresses a common or significant misconception or mistake
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Warning callout".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Warning callout > When not to use a warning callout
title: Warning callout: When not to use a warning callout
statement: Do not use a warning callout in transactional journeys as we have not tested them there, but you can use a panel if you need an interruption page if you need to tell a user to contact their GP or get medical help – use the pattern to help users decide when and where to get care (care cards) instead if the information is not important enough for a warning callout – use inset text instead
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Warning callout".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Warning callout > How to use a warning callout
title: Warning callout: How to use a warning callout
statement: Try to give the callout a short, clearly worded heading. Headings help people scan the page for warnings and understand what's relevant to them. Make the callout concise, specific and self-contained. For example, do not introduce a callout with the words "If this happens...". Explain the circumstances. Avoid having more than 2 callouts on a page. We want to reassure people, not to scare them.
citation: NHS England. NHS digital service manual, "Warning callout".

author: NHS England
subcategory: Warning callout > How to use a warning callout > Placing warning callouts
title: Warning callout: Placing warning callouts
statement: Do not break the flow with a callout. Think about whether you need it and the best place to put it.
